client: Lately, I’ve been feeling really disconnected during family gatherings. Ever since my grandma passed six months ago, it feels like everyone else has moved on, but I’m still stuck in this heavy sadness. I’m not sure if therapy can really help me feel like part of the family again—it’s like I’m just going through the motions when I’m with them.
therapist:
I hear how deeply you're still grieving your grandma's loss, and how isolating it feels when others seem to have moved forward. The way your voice tightens as you describe this makes me wonder—are you holding back tears when you're with your family, even while putting on a brave face?  

What thoughts come up when you notice yourself "going through the motions" with them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I do hold back tears. It feels like everyone expects me to be over it by now, so I just pretend I’m fine. When I’m going through the motions, I keep thinking, “Why can’t they see how much I’m still hurting?” It’s like they’ve moved on, and I’m stuck here, drowning in it. Sometimes I wonder if I’m just being too sensitive or holding onto it too long.
therapist: Your voice shakes as you share this—it sounds like there’s both pain and frustration tangled up in this grief, especially around feeling unseen. That thought, "Why can’t they see?"—do you ever test that belief, or does the fear of being "too sensitive" keep you from sharing how you really feel?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I do feel like I’m "too sensitive" sometimes, and it makes me hesitate to share how I really feel. I worry that if I speak up, people will judge me or just dismiss me as being dramatic. It’s hard because I want to be understood, but I’m afraid of being vulnerable and getting hurt even more.
therapist: The way your voice gets quieter and faster when you talk about this tells me how much this fear of judgment weighs on you. When you say you worry about being "dramatic," is that something someone told you before, or is it more a story you’ve started telling yourself about how others might react?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I think it’s a bit of both. When I was younger, my parents would tell me I was overreacting whenever I got upset about things. Now, I hear their voices in my head whenever I feel like I’m being too emotional. It’s hard to shake that feeling, like I’m always being dramatic or making a big deal out of nothing. I guess I’ve internalized it, but it still feels like it’s coming from outside me too.
therapist:
It sounds like those early messages from your parents have stayed with you, shaping how you see your emotions even now. There’s a lot of energy in your voice as you talk about this—it seems like this belief that you’re "too emotional" feels both familiar and frustrating.  

When you notice those voices in your head, do you ever pause to ask yourself if they’re still true, or if your feelings might be valid even if they’re big?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
Honestly, when I try to question those voices, it just makes me feel worse. Like I'm being disloyal to my parents by doubting what they taught me. Their words feel wired into me—I don't know who I'd be without that critical voice in my head.  

And when you say my feelings might be valid... I get what you're trying to do, but it's hard to believe that. The second I start feeling too much, I just hear my dad saying "Stop being dramatic" all over again.
therapist:
Your voice gets so quiet when you talk about this—it sounds like even questioning those beliefs brings up guilt, like you're betraying your parents. That loyalty you feel to them seems to be tangled up with the pain of their criticism.  

When your dad's voice pops up now, does it ever soften with time, or does it still feel as sharp as it did when you were younger?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
It still feels just as sharp, honestly. Sometimes I'll catch myself hearing his exact tone when I make a mistake at work - that same disappointed "I expected better from you" voice. The worst part is I know he'd deny ever being that harsh if I brought it up now. 

I guess part of me still believes he was right to be disappointed in me, even though logically I know that's messed up. But admitting that feels like I'm being ungrateful for everything they've done for me.
therapist:
The way your voice changes when you talk about your dad—it seems like this disappointment still hits hard, even years later. That conflict between knowing logically it's "messed up" and feeling like you owe them gratitude—that must feel like an impossible knot to untangle.  

When you hear his voice now, do you ever notice moments where you might react differently than younger you would have, even if the guilt still lingers?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
It's weird—sometimes I'll hear him make one of his usual sarcastic comments and I don't immediately shrink like I used to. But then the guilt crashes over me like, "Who are you to judge him after everything he's done for us?" It's exhausting going back and forth like that.  

I guess part of me still hopes if I just act grateful enough, he'll finally be the dad I needed. Isn't that pathetic?
therapist:
I hear how tired you are of this back-and-forth—holding onto that hope while also carrying the weight of guilt. The way your voice lifts when you mention not shrinking anymore suggests part of you *is* changing, even if the guilt tries to pull you back.  

That word "pathetic" lands hard—would you talk to a friend the way you're talking about yourself right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
You're right, I *wouldn't* talk to a friend like this. But that's the thing—I can't seem to extend that kindness to myself. When I try, it feels fake, like I'm just making excuses for my failures. 

The guilt is worse at night. I lie there replaying everything I should've done differently, and the self-hatred just feels... deserved, you know? Like if I stop punishing myself, I'm letting myself off too easy.
therapist:
It sounds like extending kindness to yourself feels like letting yourself off the hook—like you’re afraid if you soften toward yourself, you’ll stop holding yourself accountable.  

When those nighttime thoughts come up, do you ever notice patterns in what you feel you "should’ve" done differently? Are they always tied to your dad’s expectations, or do they branch into other areas of your life too?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
It's not just about my dad's expectations—it's everything. I lie awake thinking about how I should have been more productive at work, or how I should have been a better friend. The guilt just spreads to every part of my life. 

But when you talk about softening toward myself, it almost feels dangerous. Like if I stop punishing myself for these things, I'll just become lazy or selfish.
therapist:
The urgency in your voice tells me how real this fear is—that self-punishment might be the only thing keeping you from becoming "lazy or selfish." That belief carries so much weight.  

What would it look like to test that idea—not by dropping all accountability at once, but by experimenting with small moments of self-kindness? Could there be a middle ground between punishing yourself and letting everything go?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I get what you're saying, but it feels risky to let go of that self-punishment, even a little. What if I stop pushing myself so hard and then I actually *do* become lazy or selfish? It’s like I’ve built this wall to keep those things out, and I’m scared to even peek over it. Small moments of self-kindness sound nice in theory, but I worry they’ll just make me complacent or careless.
therapist: It sounds like that fear of becoming "complacent or careless" feels very real—like self-punishment is the only thing holding you together. The way your voice tightens when you talk about this makes me wonder: has there ever been a time when you *did* show yourself kindness, even accidentally, and things didn’t fall apart?
